why_correct: The astrologer had knifed a man in a village quarrel, thrown him into a well and fled, believing he had killed him. He never went home again, and that flight is what put him under the tamarind tree in a strange town.

why_wrong.0: He had no education and no interest in getting one. Narayan is careful to tell us he knew nothing of the stars and lived entirely by his wits.
why_wrong.2: The army is never mentioned. His trade was chosen because it needed no capital and no training, not because of any service.
why_wrong.3: He is not a priest and makes no claim to be. His turban, his vermilion and his cowrie shells are a costume for a business.

why_correct: Narayan tells us plainly that the astrologer's success came from shrewd guesswork and a lifetime of studying faces and troubles. Within five minutes of listening he knew what a customer wanted to hear.

why_wrong.0: He had run away from the fields precisely to avoid a life of farming. His trade is the opposite of that.
why_wrong.1: He had no magical power at all, and knew it. The story's irony is that a complete fraud delivers, by accident, the one true and life-changing reading of his career.
why_wrong.3: He does not practise medicine. His prescriptions are sacred ash and charms, not remedies.

why_correct: Guru Nayak had come looking for the man who stabbed him and left him for dead, meaning to kill him in return. The whole tension of the story is that he is sitting opposite that very man and does not know it.

why_wrong.0: He speaks of no lost wealth. He offers money rather than seeking it.
why_wrong.1: There is no missing brother in the story. He seeks an enemy, not a relative.
why_wrong.3: No child is involved. The astrologer's own wife and child appear only at the very end, at home.

why_correct: Nivedita records that Swamiji's love of India was total and reverent. He spoke of her past with pride and of her future with hope, and he wished his disciples to feel the same devotion.

why_wrong.0: Indifference is the opposite of everything Nivedita describes. India was the subject he returned to constantly.
why_wrong.2: He felt no fear for India. He was critical of her weaknesses, but criticism from love is not fear.
why_wrong.3: He grieved over poverty and superstition, so there is a grain of truth in disappointment, but Nivedita's account is of pride and devotion, not despondency.

why_correct: For Swamiji India was not a territory but the Divine Mother herself, an object of worship. Nivedita describes him teaching her to see the country in exactly that light.

why_wrong.0: A political unit is what a map shows. Swamiji's vision was religious, and he spoke of India as a living presence rather than a state.
why_wrong.1: Commerce plays no part in his idea of India. He measured her by her spiritual inheritance.
why_wrong.3: Military power is not his theme either. His call was to strength of character and of soul.

why_correct: The Amarnath pilgrimage crosses high and difficult mountain country in Kashmir, and Nivedita's account dwells on the hard climbing, the cold and the exhaustion of the road.

why_wrong.0: There is no desert on the route. The hardship of Amarnath is altitude and ice, not sand.
why_wrong.2: No sea is crossed. The whole journey is inland and upward.
why_wrong.3: Forest is passed on the lower slopes, but what the pilgrims struggle with is the mountain path itself.

why_correct: What struck Nivedita most deeply was Swamiji's own experience inside the cave. He came out shaken and transfigured, and she writes that he felt he had been granted a vision of Shiva.

why_wrong.0: No market figures in the account. The journey is a pilgrimage, not a visit to a town.
why_wrong.1: The cave and its ice lingam are impressive, and she describes them, but her attention is fixed on what happened to Swamiji there. The question asks what impressed her most.
why_wrong.3: Local rulers play no part in the episode.

why_correct: Wordsworth sees London in the early morning before it wakes. The houses seem asleep and the mighty heart is lying still, so the city appears calm and at peace.

why_wrong.0: Noise and crowds are what London would be at any other hour, which is exactly the contrast the poet is drawing. He catches it at the one moment it is silent.
why_wrong.2: The city is not dark. It is bright and bare in the smokeless air, glittering in the first sunlight.
why_wrong.3: Smokeless is Wordsworth's own word. He is struck by how clean the air is at that hour.

why_correct: The city wears the beauty of the morning like a garment. The image makes the beauty something put on, temporary and fitting, which is why the moment must be caught before the day begins.

why_wrong.0: No jewel appears in the poem. Wordsworth's images are of clothing, of open fields and of a sleeping body.
why_wrong.2: The river glideth at his own sweet will, so the Thames is in the poem, but as one of the things seen rather than as the comparison for the city's beauty.
why_wrong.3: Towers, domes, theatres and temples are listed, but they are the city itself and not what its beauty is likened to.

why_correct: The whole sonnet is an act of stillness: silent, bare, calm, and a deep, sweet-tasting quiet. Serenity is the quality of nature that Wordsworth finds unexpectedly in the middle of a great city.

why_wrong.0: There is no violence anywhere in the poem.
why_wrong.1: Restlessness is what a city normally offers and what the poem is a relief from. Judge by the words: calm, still, asleep.
why_wrong.3: The scene is clear rather than mysterious. Wordsworth can see everything, all bright and glittering, which is part of the wonder.

why_correct: Sarojini Naidu's silver and blue bangles are for the maiden, likened to mountain mist and the bud of a new-born leaf. They stand for a girl on the edge of womanhood.

why_wrong.0: Childhood is not one of the stages the poem sets out. It moves from maiden to bride to matron.
why_wrong.2: The bangles are cheap glass, carried to a village fair. Wealth is not what they signify.
why_wrong.3: The poem has no sorrow in it. Even the last stanza, on the older woman, is written with dignity and warmth.

why_correct: The bride's bangles are flame-bright, likened to the fire of her marriage and to her bridal laughter and tears. Red and gold, they carry the colour of the wedding fire itself.

why_wrong.0: Mountain mist belongs to the maiden's silver and blue bangles, not the bride's.
why_wrong.1: Flowers appear as images elsewhere in Naidu's work but not for the bride's bangles here.
why_wrong.3: Morning clouds again suit the pale colours of the maiden's stanza. The bride's stanza is deliberately hot and bright by contrast.

why_correct: The poem's three stanzas of bangles correspond to three stages of a woman's life: the maiden, the bride and the mother who has raised her children. The bangle seller's tray is a way of showing a whole life.

why_wrong.0: Nothing industrial appears. The bangles are handmade and sold at a village fair.
why_wrong.2: There is no war and no heroism in the poem.
why_wrong.3: Naidu was a political figure, but this poem is not political. Its subject is domestic life.

why_correct: Yeats opens with the falcon turning in a widening gyre and unable to hear the falconer. The trained bird has lost touch with its master, which is his image for a civilisation that has lost its centre.

why_wrong.0: Falconry is the image, and the man who flies the bird is the falconer. A hunter is a different figure.
why_wrong.2: There is no shepherd in the poem. The rough beast of the second stanza is the only animal besides the falcon.
why_wrong.3: No king appears. The authority that has failed is not political but something deeper.

why_correct: Things fall apart, the centre cannot hold. Yeats is describing a world whose old order is disintegrating, with anarchy loosed and the best lacking all conviction while the worst are full of passionate intensity.

why_wrong.0: Perfect order is precisely what the poem says has ended.
why_wrong.1: The poem describes the opposite of stability. Written just after the First World War, it is a vision of collapse.
why_wrong.3: There is no peace. The poem ends with a rough beast slouching towards Bethlehem, which is a threat rather than a consolation.

why_correct: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and the equal protection of the laws. It opens the Right to Equality, which runs from Article 14 to Article 18.

why_wrong.1: Article 19 gives the six freedoms, including speech and expression, and belongs to the Right to Freedom.
why_wrong.2: Article 21 protects life and personal liberty, the article on which much of modern Indian rights law is built. Also under the Right to Freedom.
why_wrong.3: Article 32 is the right to constitutional remedies, which Ambedkar called the heart and soul of the Constitution. It is the way to enforce the other rights, not a right to equality.

why_correct: UNESCO has its headquarters in Paris, where it was founded in 1946. It is the UN agency for education, science and culture, and it maintains the World Heritage list.

why_wrong.0: Geneva houses the WHO, the ILO and the UN Office at Geneva, so it is a major UN city but not UNESCO's home.
why_wrong.1: New York is the headquarters of the United Nations itself. The agency and the parent body are in different cities, which is the point of the question.
why_wrong.3: Vienna hosts the International Atomic Energy Agency and the UN Office at Vienna.

why_correct: Mars is the Red Planet, coloured by the iron oxide dust that covers its surface. That is simply rust, and it is visible even to the naked eye from Earth.

why_wrong.0: Venus is the hottest planet, veiled in thick sulphuric acid cloud, and appears whitish yellow.
why_wrong.2: Jupiter is the largest planet and shows bands of cream and brown. Its Great Red Spot is a storm, not the planet's colour.
why_wrong.3: Saturn is the ringed planet, pale gold in colour.

why_correct: Mother Teresa won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 for her work with the destitute and dying in Kolkata. She was an Indian citizen, which is what makes her the first Indian woman to receive the prize.

why_wrong.0: Indira Gandhi was Prime Minister and won the Bharat Ratna, but never a Nobel Prize.
why_wrong.2: Sarojini Naidu was a poet and freedom fighter called the Nightingale of India, and the first woman governor of an Indian state. Many firsts, but not this one.
why_wrong.3: Kalpana Chawla was the first woman of Indian origin in space. An astronaut, not a Nobel laureate.

why_correct: The Blue Revolution refers to the rapid growth of fish production and aquaculture in India. Blue for water, and it is associated with Dr Hiralal Chaudhuri.

why_wrong.0: Milk is the White Revolution, or Operation Flood, led by Dr Verghese Kurien. The best known of these colour revolutions and the usual wrong answer here.
why_wrong.3: Poultry and eggs are the Silver Revolution. It is worth learning the whole set together: green for food grains, white for milk, blue for fish, yellow for oilseeds.

why_correct: Gujarat has the longest coastline of any Indian state, about 1,600 kilometres, because of the deeply indented shores of the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gulf of Khambhat.

why_wrong.0: Tamil Nadu has a long coast of roughly 1,000 kilometres, but a much straighter one.
why_wrong.1: Andhra Pradesh is second at about 970 kilometres after the separation of Telangana.
why_wrong.3: Maharashtra's Konkan coast runs about 720 kilometres. Note that the longest coastline of any Indian territory belongs to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, but that is a union territory, not a state.

why_correct: The currency of Japan is the yen. Its symbol is a Y with two strokes, and it is one of the most traded currencies in the world.

why_wrong.0: The won is the currency of South Korea and, separately, of North Korea.
why_wrong.1: The yuan is the currency of China, more formally the renminbi. Yuan and yen are easily confused because both descend from the same Chinese word for a round coin.
why_wrong.3: The ringgit is the currency of Malaysia.

why_correct: Jawaharlal Nehru wrote The Discovery of India in 1944 while imprisoned at Ahmednagar Fort. He also wrote Glimpses of World History and an autobiography.

why_wrong.0: Gandhi wrote The Story of My Experiments with Truth and Hind Swaraj.
why_wrong.1: Ambedkar wrote Annihilation of Caste and The Problem of the Rupee.
why_wrong.3: Patel was not an author of note. Nehru is the one of these four remembered as much for his books as for his politics.

why_correct: The Antarctic is the largest desert in the world, about 14 million square kilometres. A desert is defined by how little precipitation it receives, not by heat, and Antarctica is the driest place on Earth.

why_wrong.0: The Sahara, about 9 million square kilometres, is the largest hot desert, and that is the answer most people give. The question asks for the largest of all deserts, and the two polar deserts are bigger.
why_wrong.1: The Gobi, in Mongolia and China, is a cold desert but far smaller, about 1.3 million square kilometres.
why_wrong.2: The Arabian Desert is roughly 2.3 million square kilometres, large but well short of the Sahara, let alone Antarctica.

why_correct: The International Court of Justice sits at the Peace Palace in The Hague, in the Netherlands. It is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations and settles disputes between states.

why_wrong.0: Geneva houses many UN agencies but not the Court.
why_wrong.2: Brussels is the seat of the European Union and of NATO, neither of which is a UN body.
why_wrong.3: Washington D.C. is the headquarters of the World Bank and the IMF. Note that the ICJ is the only principal organ of the UN not based in New York.
